newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian share prices set to slide further.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian share prices set to slide further.

text.p: Share prices on the Nigerian stock market are poised to slide for some time, analysts said on Thursday.
They blame the bearish trend on a general misunderstanding of the recently introduced central clearing system and a combination of factors.
The market's all-share index which rose above 8800 a month ago had shrunk to 8621.43 by Wednesday.

"There has been an alteration of trading practices following the introduction of the CSCS (central securities clearing system) due to a general misuderstanding of the working of the system," Bayo Adeniji of brokerage house Hamilton Hammer, told Reuters.
He said many dealers who used to make prices without having the funds to back them under the old system were now unable to do so and had chosen to wait and see how it worked out.

Dealers can now only trade up to the amount they have in their stockbroking account, which the stock exchange has access to under the clearing system. Those who exceed the amount in their account face sanctions.
The computerised clearing system, intended to remove constraints to the influx of foreign capital and increase turnover, came into operation last month.
But market operators complain they need more time to understand it.
"If the managers of CSCS agree that they need more consultations and time, it will work," Tola Mobolurin, chief executive of trading company Capital Bancorp, said.
Consultation so far by the authorities has been inadequate, Mobolurin said at a seminar this week.
According to Adeniji, funds which found their way into shares when interest rates fell were returning to the money market as rates rose again.
"This has led to a flurry to sell shares in recent weeks," he said.
Interest rates which went as low as three percent two months ago are now hovering around 21 percent.
Rates were previously fixed by the government at 21 percent until they were freed last year.
Adeniji said the situation would correct itself with time but could not say how long it would take.
"There tends to be a bandwagon effect in any market all over the world but it will normalise over a period of time. How long that will be, I cannot say."
Some operators also believe the shares were bound to fall, saying they were over-valued.
Mostly affected are bank and oil marketing shares which have risen sharply since last year.
First Bank, which has nearly trippled in value since January when its lowest price was 7.10 naira, has been sliding consistently and traded at 13.90 naira on Wednesday.
Also, oil marketer Total closed at 59.50 naira on Wednesday against a year's high of 73.05 naira.
One trader said shares would have to fall to between 50 percent and 70 percent below their current prices.
($1=85 naira)
